summary: JSONPath is a string syntax for selecting and extracting values from within a JSON value (RFC 8259). It works like a query language for JSON documents. This document standardizes a syntax that many earlier informal implementations differed on.

eli5.summary: If you have a giant box of boxes, JSONPath is a short address like "third box, second item" that gets you straight to what you want.

questions: what does the jsonpath double dot mean
subtitle: A standard query language for picking values out of a JSON document, with precise rules where old implementations disagreed.

tldr.problem: JSONPath began as an informal 2007 proposal, and implementations often handed parts of a query to the host language's engine, so the same query behaved differently from one library to the next.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9535 defines a grammar and exact semantics: a query starts at the root $, applies child and descendant segments built from name, wildcard, index, slice and filter selectors, and returns a list of nodes. Filters can call a typed set of function extensions.
tldr.outcome: There is now one normative JSONPath that does not depend on any programming language, including a registry for new functions, a Normalized Path form and a media type, application/jsonpath.

today: RFC 9535 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2024, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the normative JSONPath specification, relying on RFC 9485 for regular expressions.

sections.title: What JSONPath Is and Where It Came From
sections.content:
JSONPath defines a string syntax for selecting and extracting JSON values (RFC 8259) from within a given JSON value. It is meant as a more powerful companion to JSON Pointer (RFC 6901), not a replacement.

The document builds on Stefan Gössner's popular 2007 proposal and the experience of its widespread implementations. JSONPath was originally a lightweight companion to JSON in languages such as PHP and JavaScript, so it delegated parts of a query to the host runtime, for example JavaScript's own code-evaluation function. As more environments implemented it, expressions became decreasingly portable. For example, regular expression processing was often delegated to whatever engine was convenient.

RFC 9535 aims to remove such implementation-specific dependencies. It admits that backwards compatibility is not always achieved: the design principle is to follow a rough "consensus" between implementations, as long as that does not jeopardize a usable, stable JSON query language. The name comes from XPath, which inspired it, and from the fact that a query's outcome consists of paths identifying nodes.
sections.eli5: People made many different versions of the same treasure-map language, and the maps meant different things in different places. This RFC writes one official rulebook.

sections.title: Values, Nodes and Nodelists
sections.content:
A JSONPath expression is applied to a JSON value, the query argument, and its output is a nodelist. A node is a value together with its location in the query argument. The root node is the one whose value is the entire argument. The children of an array node are its elements, and the children of an object node are its member values.

Only member values have nodes. Member names and members (name/value pairs) cannot be selected. A query is a sequence of Unicode scalar values and MUST be encoded in UTF-8.

A query must be both well-formed (it matches the ABNF) and valid (integers are within the I-JSON range of exact values, namely [-(2^53)+1, (2^53)-1], and function uses are well-typed). An implementation MUST raise an error for a query that is not both. Both properties depend only on the query, never on the data, so mismatches with the data show up only as empty results, and an empty nodelist is a valid result.

Where the input is not interoperable JSON, such as objects with duplicate member names, behavior is unpredictable and the RFC does not try to define it. Resource exhaustion is not modeled, but an implementation MUST NOT silently malfunction and MUST indicate overflow.
sections.eli5: The whole JSON document is a tree. A query walks over the tree and hands back a list of the spots it landed on. If it finds nothing, it hands back an empty list, which is not a mistake.

sections.title: Queries, Identifiers and Segments
sections.content:
A query is a root identifier $ followed by zero or more segments. Each segment is applied to every node in the previous nodelist, and the results are concatenated in order. A node selected more than once appears that many times, because duplicates are not removed. If any segment yields an empty nodelist, the whole query does.

There are two kinds of segment. A child segment [<selectors>] selects children of each input node. A descendant segment ..[<selectors>] visits the input node and each of its descendants, nodes before their descendants and arrays in order, and applies the child segment to each. Bracket notation is canonical. Shorthands exist: .name means ['name'], .* means [*], ..name means ..['name'] and ..* means ..[*]. Dot shorthand works only for member names made of the characters the grammar permits, so $.foo.bar is $['foo']['bar'] but not $['foo.bar'].

A syntactically valid segment MUST NOT produce errors during evaluation. An index beyond the end of an array simply selects fewer nodes. JSON null is an ordinary value, not "missing", and $.null refers to a member named "null".
sections.eli5: A query starts at the top of the box and then follows steps. Each step opens the next level of boxes, either just one level down or any number of levels down.

sections.title: Name, Wildcard, Index and Slice Selectors
sections.content:
The name selector 'name' selects at most one member value. Unlike JSON, strings may use single or double quotes. Names are compared as identical sequences of Unicode scalar values, and no normalization is applied. The wildcard selector an asterisk selects all children of an object or array, and nothing from a primitive value. The order of an object's children is not stipulated, because JSON objects are unordered.

The index selector is a base-10 integer with no leading zeros. It is zero-based, so 0 is the first element. A negative index counts back from the end, so -1 is the last element. An index outside the array selects nothing and is not an error.

The array slice selector start:end:step takes elements from start up to but not including end, moving by step, which defaults to 1. For example, 1:3 selects indices 1 and 2, 1:5:2 selects indices 1 and 3, and 5:1:-2 selects indices 5 and 3. A step of -1 with the other parts empty (::-1) reverses the array. A step of 0 selects nothing, which differs from Python, where it is an error.

A child segment can hold several comma-separated selectors of different kinds, and their results are concatenated in order. Selecting the same node twice, as in $[0, 0], yields it twice.
sections.eli5: You can pick a thing by its name, grab everything, pick the nth item counting from either end, or take every other item in a stretch.

sections.title: Filter Selectors
sections.content:
The filter selector ?<logical-expr> goes through the elements of an array or the member values of an object, and keeps those for which the logical expression is true. On a primitive value it selects nothing. Inside the expression, @ is the current node. It always refers to the directly enclosing filter, and there is no syntax for the node of an outer filter. Expressions combine with ||, && and !, and parentheses are allowed. Precedence from highest to lowest is grouping and function expressions, !, comparisons, &&, then ||. The old requirement to wrap the expression in parentheses is gone.

A query on its own in a logical context is an existence test: true if it selects at least one node. To look at a node's value you must compare it, for example @.foo == null, because the test !@.foo only reports whether a node exists.

Comparisons (==, !=, <, <=, >, >=) work on literals, singular queries (queries that select at most one node) and functions returning values. Two empty results are equal to each other, and any < involving an empty result is false. Numbers compare mathematically, strings by Unicode scalar values, and arrays and objects can be tested for equality but are not ordered. Different types never compare equal, so 13 == '13' is false. For example, $.store.book[?@.price < 10].title selects the titles of books under 10.
sections.eli5: A filter is a yes-or-no question asked about each item, like "is this book cheaper than 10?". Only items that get a yes make it into the answer.

sections.title: Function Extensions and IANA Registries
sections.content:
Filters can call function extensions. Each has a unique lowercase name, typed parameters and a typed result, and its evaluation MUST be free of side effects. There are three declared types: ValueType (a JSON value or the special result Nothing), LogicalType (LogicalTrue or LogicalFalse, unrelated to JSON true and false) and NodesType (a nodelist). A nodelist converts to logical (non-empty means true), but there is no implicit conversion to a value. The value() function exists for that. Because types are declared, well-typedness can be checked from the query alone. For example, $[?match(@.timezone, 'Europe/.*') == true] is not well-typed, because LogicalType cannot be used in a comparison.

Five functions are built in: length() (characters of a string, elements of an array or members of an object), count() (nodes in a nodelist, without deduplication), match() (whole-string regular expression match), search() (substring match) and value() (the value of a single node, otherwise Nothing). Both regular-expression functions use I-Regexp (RFC 9485) and return LogicalFalse if the pattern is not valid I-Regexp.

IANA registered the media type application/jsonpath and created a "Function Extensions" subregistry in a new "JSONPath" registry, with the policy Expert Review. The experts are told to be frugal with generally suggestive names.
sections.eli5: Filters can use little helper tools, like one that counts things or checks a word's pattern. Each tool says what it takes in and what it gives back, so a mix-up is caught before the search even starts.

sections.title: Normalized Paths
sections.content:
A Normalized Path is a restricted JSONPath query that identifies exactly one node in a specific value. Every node has precisely one. It uses bracket notation, single-quoted names and non-negative indexes only, with fixed escaping rules so there is only one way to write it. For example, $[-3] on an array of length 5 normalizes to $[2], and $.a.b[1:2] normalizes to $['a']['b'][1].

Normalized Paths are singular queries, but not every singular query is one. They give a predictable format for testing and for post-processing a nodelist, for example removing duplicates. A nodelist can be written compactly as an array of Normalized Path strings, and the RFC's own examples use them as result paths.
sections.eli5: A Normalized Path is the one official street address of a spot in the document, with no nicknames allowed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC names three areas of risk. First, implementations: handing query parts to a language engine, such as JavaScript's code-evaluation function, is known to cause injection attacks, so implementations need to parse the whole syntax themselves. Attackers may also craft queries or data that cost exponential CPU time, or that overflow the stack in a naive recursive descendant segment, so implementations need appropriate resource management.

Second, query construction: queries are often built from variables such as names and comparison values. These must be validated and escaped, otherwise an adversary controlling them, for example through a web form, can cause injection attacks like SQL injection.

Third, security mechanisms that use JSONPath: attackers can try to exploit differences in behavior between implementations, unpredictable inputs, or the behavior of underlying technologies such as UTF-8 and Unicode. For query arguments conforming to I-JSON (RFC 7493), behavior is predictable except for the ordering of objects.
sections.eli5: Never paste strangers' words straight into your search directions, because they could sneak in tricks. Check and clean everything first.
